{0}{1}Make a flood plan

What to move, what to switch off, where to go. When a flood warning comes there's little time. Decide now what you'd move upstairs, how to turn off the gas, electricity and water, and where you'd go. And never drive through floodwater: {0}cm of flowing water can float a car.
{0}{1}Sign up for free flood warnings
By text, phone or email. You'll get a warning when flooding is expected where you live, often hours before the water arrives. You can sign up a relative too.
{0}{1}Keep documents and medicines in a waterproof bag
A sealed freezer bag works. Floodwater ruins paper and medicine. Keep passports, insurance details and a few days of medicine sealed, upstairs or in your grab bag.
{0}{1}Check your insurance covers flooding
Look at your policy, or ask your insurer. Check your buildings and contents cover include flood damage. If cover is hard to find because of flood risk, ask your insurer about Flood Re.

If the water goes off or isn't safe to drink, you need about {0} litres per person per day for drinking, plus some for cooking and washing. Supermarkets sell out within hours.
Keep {0} days of bottled water: for {1} people that's {2} large {3}-litre bottles.
Buy a few bottles each shop, and keep them somewhere cool and dark.
Use the oldest first and replace them, so they never go out of date.
Tap water in clean, sealed bottles lasts {0} months. Write the date on them.

When the power and mobile signal go, local radio is how you hear what's happening, where to go and when it will be fixed.
Get a battery or wind-up radio.
Find your local station and write the frequency on it.
Keep spare batteries with it.

Food that needs no cooking
In a power cut, cookers, microwaves and fridges stop. Food that's ready to eat keeps everyone going.
Keep {0} days of food you can eat cold: tins, crackers, cereal, peanut butter, dried fruit.
Keep a manual tin opener with it.
Rotate it into your normal meals, so nothing goes out of date.
Supermarket own-brand tins cost less than £{0} each.
A torch, and spare batteries
Candles cause house fires during power cuts. A torch is safer, and phone torches flatten the battery you need for calls.
Keep a torch where you can find it in the dark, like the kitchen drawer.
Check it works when the clocks change.
Torches cost from about £{0}. A wind-up torch needs no batteries.
Your phone is how you call for help and hear from family. In a long power cut, it won't last a day without a top-up.
Keep a power bank charged, and charge it again every few months.
Keep the right cable with it.
In a power cut, use low power mode and keep calls short.
A basic power bank costs about £{0}.
Keeping warm without heating
Most heating stops in a power cut, and a cold home is dangerous for older people and babies.
Keep blankets or sleeping bags, hats and thick socks for everyone.
Choose one room to keep warm, and close the doors.
Never use a gas cooker or barbecue to heat a room.
Charity shops are a good place for blankets.
In an emergency, help can take longer to arrive. A basic kit deals with cuts and burns until it does.
Keep a first aid kit in the kitchen.
Check it's complete and in date.
Consider a free or low-cost first aid course: the Red Cross and St John Ambulance run them.
Basic kits cost about £{0} to £{1}.
Fires and carbon monoxide are more likely during power cuts and cold snaps, when people use candles, heaters and generators.
Fit a smoke alarm on each floor.
Fit a carbon monoxide alarm in rooms with a gas or solid fuel appliance.
Test them monthly.
Your fire and rescue service may fit alarms for free with a home safety visit.
When the power or internet is down, card machines and cash machines stop working.
Keep some cash in small notes and coins.
Keep it somewhere safe, with your documents.
Top it up if you use it.
Even £{0} in small notes helps.
If you have to leave home quickly, for a flood or a fire, there's no time to think about what to take.
Pack a bag with medicines, chargers, documents, a torch, water and snacks.
Keep it by the door or upstairs.
Tell everyone at home where it is.
Use a bag you already have.
Pharmacies can close in bad weather and power cuts, and deliveries stop.
Order repeat prescriptions a week before you run out.
Keep a list of medicines and doses on paper.
Ask the pharmacist what to do with medicines kept in the fridge.
Free: it's about ordering in time.
Someone to check on you
In an emergency, people living alone are the most at risk, and phones may not work.
Agree with a neighbour or relative that they'll knock on your door.
Swap numbers, and write them on paper too.
Agree a sign, like a card in the window, if you need help.
The Environment Agency can warn you hours before flooding, by text, phone or email.
Sign up at gov.uk/sign-up-for-flood-warnings, or call Floodline on {0} {1} {2}.
Do it for older relatives too, with their agreement.
When a flood warning comes there may be only a few hours, often at night. A plan means the decisions are made.
Find out how to turn off gas, electricity and water.
Decide what you'd move upstairs first.
Decide where you'd go, and how you'd get there without driving through water.
